title: Clickjacking and Framing
summary: Clickjacking steals a click, not a credential: your real page, invisible, under bait UI. Learn how framing attacks work and why frame-ancestors is the header that actually stops them.

slides.markdown:
**Clickjacking** — the formal name is *UI redress* — is the attack where a user genuinely clicks a real button on your real site, having been shown something entirely different on screen.

There's no injection, no stolen token, and nothing malformed about any request. Your page loads normally inside an iframe on the attacker's site, gets rendered invisible, and is positioned so that the button the victim thinks they're clicking sits exactly over the one that matters — Confirm, Authorise, Delete, Grant access.

Because the click is real and the session is real, every server-side control passes. CSRF tokens are present, `SameSite` is satisfied, the `Origin` is your own. **The defense has to be "don't let other sites frame me,"** which is a single response header.

That header is `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors`, with `X-Frame-Options` as the legacy version — and the frontend interview version of this topic is usually "how do you stop this page being embedded elsewhere."

slides.subTitle: Why every server-side check passes
slides.markdown:
The mechanism is entirely visual, built from ordinary CSS:

- The attacker's page embeds your page in an `<iframe>`.
- CSS makes that frame effectively invisible — near-zero opacity, or positioned under another element — while it remains fully interactive. Invisible and clickable are independent properties in CSS.
- Bait content is laid out underneath so that something the user *wants* to click sits precisely beneath your consequential button.
- The user clicks. The event goes to your framed page, from your origin, in their logged-in session.

Now look at it from your server's perspective. The request is a genuine action, from a real session, with a valid CSRF token that your own page supplied, and an `Origin` header naming *you* — because the click really did happen on your page. Nothing distinguishes it from a legitimate action, because at the HTTP layer it **is** one.

That's why no request-level control helps, and why the only durable fix is refusing to be framed. The victim's intent was subverted before the request existed.

Picture the same rectangle of screen, drawn twice.

**What the user sees:** a bright page with an obvious call to action — "Claim your prize," "Play video," "Continue." Nothing about it looks unusual, and the URL bar shows the attacker's domain, which the user has no particular reason to distrust.

**What is actually on top:** your page, in a transparent iframe, scrolled and offset so its "Transfer" or "Authorise app" button is exactly under the bait button. The frame is the topmost layer in stacking order, so it receives the click.

**What the user's finger does:** lands on the bait, and the event is delivered to your page.

Two details make it durable in practice. The alignment can be adjusted per browser and viewport, so it works across devices. And the attacker can follow the victim's cursor, moving the frame so the target sits under the pointer wherever it goes — which defeats "the user would have to click in exactly the right spot."

slides.sectionTitle: What a stolen click is worth
slides.markdown:
A single click sounds cheap until you list the one-click actions in a typical product.

- **OAuth consent.** "Allow this app to read your email" is one button. A stolen click there grants an attacker-controlled application durable API access — no password, no session theft, and it survives the user logging out.
- **Enabling a device or camera permission** in an app-level settings toggle.
- **Adding a payment method or confirming a purchase** where the flow ends in a single confirm.
- **Changing a privacy setting to public**, which is the original "likejacking" family that spread across social networks around 2010 and is why those platforms were early adopters of framing headers.
- **Deleting a resource**, where a confirm dialog is itself just another button to align under.
- **Multi-click sequences.** The attacker can reposition the frame between clicks, so a flow requiring three confirmations is harder but not immune.

The severity rule follows: rate a clickjacking finding by **what your most consequential single-click action is**, not by how fiddly the attack looks. A page with no state-changing controls is genuinely low risk; a page with an OAuth grant is not.

slides.subTitle: Legacy and modern
slides.markdown:
| | `X-Frame-Options` | CSP `frame-ancestors` |
|---|---|---|
| Status | legacy, obsoleted by CSP | current standard |
| Values | `DENY`, `SAMEORIGIN` | `'none'`, `'self'`, any list of origins |
| Multiple allowed origins | no — `ALLOW-FROM` was never widely supported and is deprecated | yes, that's the point |
| Wildcards / schemes | no | yes, e.g. `https://*.partner.com` |
| Deliverable via `<meta>` | no | **no** — must be a real header |
| Precedence | ignored where `frame-ancestors` is present | wins |

**Send both.** `frame-ancestors` is the one that does the work and expresses the policy you actually want; `X-Frame-Options: DENY` costs one line and covers any old client that ignores CSP. Where both are present, modern browsers honour `frame-ancestors`, so there's no conflict to reason about.

The trap worth remembering: `ALLOW-FROM` looks like the answer when you need exactly one partner to embed you, and it does not work — it was never implemented in Chrome or Safari. If you need an allowlist, you need `frame-ancestors`, full stop.

Also note `SAMEORIGIN` is origin-scoped while much else in web security is site-scoped, so it does *not* permit a different subdomain to frame you.

The blanket block, for an app that should never be embedded:

```http
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'
X-Frame-Options: DENY
```

Same-origin framing only — you use iframes internally but nobody else may embed you:

```http
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
```

A named allowlist, for a widget two specific partners embed:

```http
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://partner-a.com https://*.partner-b.com
```

In Express, as middleware applied to every HTML response:

```js
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.setHeader('Content-Security-Policy', "frame-ancestors 'none'");
  res.setHeader('X-Frame-Options', 'DENY');
  next();
});
```

Two deployment details that decide whether this works:

- **It must be on every HTML response**, including error pages, legacy routes, and anything served directly by a CDN or storage bucket that bypasses your app. Attackers look for exactly those.
- **`frame-ancestors` cannot be delivered via a `<meta>` tag.** If your only CSP is a meta tag, you have no framing protection at all, and the browser silently ignores the directive rather than warning you.

slides.subTitle: Allowlist, not a blanket block
slides.markdown:
Plenty of legitimate products exist to be embedded: a payment form, a support chat widget, a video player, an embeddable dashboard, an SSO consent screen inside a partner portal. "Just set `DENY`" is not available.

How to keep it safe anyway:

- **Allowlist explicitly, per customer.** `frame-ancestors` accepts a list, so generate the header per tenant from the parent origins that customer registered. A wildcard like `https://*` is the same as no protection.
- **Split the surface.** The embeddable page should contain only what needs embedding. Account settings, billing, and anything destructive live on pages with `frame-ancestors 'none'`. This is the highest-value structural move.
- **Require deliberate interaction for consequential actions.** Typing an amount, re-entering a card's security code, or a step-up re-auth cannot be stolen by aligning one button. Payment providers do this for exactly this reason.
- **Use `sandbox` on frames you host**, and expect your embedders to sandbox you.
- **Validate the parent origin at runtime** if you communicate over `postMessage`, and never trust a parent-supplied claim about who it is.

The general principle: framing protection is a **per-page** decision, not a per-site one. Most apps should default to `'none'` and open specific routes deliberately.

slides.subTitle: The defense that stopped working
slides.markdown:
Before the headers existed, the standard defense was a script checking whether the page was the top window and, if not, forcing itself out. Variants of it still ship in old codebases and still show up in interview answers.

It is not a defense, for a structural reason: **the attacker controls the parent frame, and the parent has ways to constrain the child.**

The families of neutralisation, at a high level — enough to know why you can't win, without a recipe:

- **Sandboxing.** An `<iframe sandbox>` without the token that permits top-level navigation prevents the framed page navigating the top window at all. Your bust script runs and its action is simply denied. This is the killer: the very attribute meant to contain untrusted content disables the defense.
- **Intercepting the navigation.** The parent can hook the events that precede a top-level navigation and cancel or redirect it.
- **Timing and race conditions.** The script runs after some rendering, and a click landing in that window still counts.
- **Client variation.** Any user without JavaScript, or with an extension interfering, has no protection at all.

Even the "best" documented frame-busting snippet — hide the page with CSS by default and reveal it only if the script confirms it's top-level — degrades to a blank page rather than to safety, and still fails against sandboxing.

**Use the headers.** Frame-busting is at most a cosmetic fallback for clients that ignore them, and honestly not worth the code.

slides.sectionTitle: Ways the header ends up missing
slides.markdown:
In practice, clickjacking findings on mature apps are almost never "we didn't know about the header." They're coverage gaps.

- **Only the app sets it.** Static assets, uploaded content, error pages, and health-check or legacy routes served by the CDN, an S3 bucket, or the load balancer never pass through your middleware. An HTML page in an assets bucket is framable.
- **Only some responses.** Setting the header on `200` responses but not on the `4xx`/`5xx` templates, which are still framable pages with your branding — and sometimes with a login form.
- **A `<meta>`-only CSP.** `frame-ancestors` is silently ignored in a meta tag. The policy looks present in the HTML and does nothing.
- **A reverse proxy stripping or overwriting it.** Two layers each setting `X-Frame-Options` can produce a duplicated or conflicting header that browsers may discard entirely.
- **`SAMEORIGIN` assumed to mean same-site.** It's origin-scoped, so a subdomain cannot frame you — which surprises teams whose own tooling lives on a different subdomain, and leads to it being loosened.
- **A new subdomain or acquisition** deployed on a stack that never inherited the standard header set.

The fix that scales: set framing headers at the **edge**, for everything, and treat any route that needs framing as an explicit exception. Then assert it in an automated test that crawls real URLs, not just the app's routes.

The header is the answer, and it's worth knowing what backs it up when the header can't apply — an embeddable surface, or a client that ignores it.

- **Design consequential actions to need more than one aligned click.** A typed confirmation, a re-entered code, or a step-up authentication cannot be harvested by positioning a button. This is why sensitive flows in banking and OAuth consent screens tend to feel deliberately slow.
- **`SameSite=Strict` on a cookie that gates destructive actions.** A framed page is a cross-site context, so a `Strict` cookie isn't sent — which can turn the stolen click into an unauthenticated request. See [csrf-from-the-frontend](csrf-from-the-frontend) for the cookie mechanics.
- **`Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`** to sever `window.opener` relationships, closing the related tabnabbing family where a popup rewrites the opener page.
- **Rate-limit and monitor** the actions that matter. A spike of one-click grants from unusual referrers is a detectable signal.
- **Keep `frame-ancestors` in the same CSP you're already shipping** — see [content-security-policy](content-security-policy) — so framing policy is reviewed alongside everything else rather than living in a forgotten header config.

The answer to give when asked: set `frame-ancestors` (plus legacy `X-Frame-Options`) at the edge on every response, default to `'none'`, allowlist per route where embedding is a real feature, and don't rely on JavaScript for any of it.
